Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Aims and Methods: We present the results of VLBI observations of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources at 1.6 GHz. Of them, 15 sources are selected from the Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample (Snellen 2002), 4 others are from our previous observation list. We aimed at imaging the structure of GPS sources, searching for Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs) and studying the absorption for the convex radio spectra of GPS sources.   Results: We obtained total intensity 1.6 GHz VLBI images of 17 sources for the first time. Of them, 80% show mini-double-lobe radio structure, indicating that they are CSOs or candidates, and their host AGNs could be edge-on to us. This result suggests that there is a high incidence of mini double-lobe sources (or CSOs) in the PHJ sample. The sources J0323+0534, J1135-0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123-0112 and J2325-0344 with measured redshift, showing double-lobe structure with sizes of <1 kpc, are classified as CSOs. Three sources J1057+0012, J1600-0037 and J1753+2750 are considered as core-jet sources according to their morphologies and flux variability.

**Aims and Methods:** We present the results of 1.6 GHz VLBI observations of nineteen GHz-peaked-spectrum (GPS) radio sources. Fifteen of these sources were selected from the Parkes Half-Jansky (PHJ) sample (Snellen 2002), while the remaining four were drawn from our previous observation list. Our objectives were to image the structures of GPS sources, search for compact symmetric objects (CSOs), and investigate the absorption responsible for the convex radio spectra of GPS sources.

**Results:** We obtained total-intensity 1.6 GHz VLBI images of 17 sources for the first time. Of these, 80% exhibit mini-double-lobe radio structures, indicating that they are CSOs or CSO candidates and that their host AGNs may be viewed edge-on. This finding suggests a high incidence of mini-double-lobe sources, or CSOs, in the PHJ sample. The sources J0323+0534, J1135−0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123−0112, and J2325−0344, which have measured redshifts and exhibit double-lobe structures smaller than 1 kpc, are classified as CSOs. Based on their morphologies and flux variability, J1057+0012, J1600−0037, and J1753+2750 are considered core–jet sources.

**Aims and Methods:** We report 1.6 GHz VLBI observations of 19 gigahertz-peaked-spectrum (GPS) radio sources. Fifteen targets were drawn from the Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample (Snellen 2002), while the remaining four came from our earlier observing list. The study sought to map the structures of GPS sources, identify compact symmetric objects (CSOs), and investigate the absorption responsible for their convex radio spectra.

**Results:** We produced the first total-intensity 1.6 GHz VLBI images for 17 of the sources. Approximately 80% exhibit compact double-lobed morphologies, implying that they are either CSOs or CSO candidates and that their host active galactic nuclei may be viewed edge-on. These findings indicate that mini double-lobed objects, including CSOs, occur frequently in the PHJ sample. Six sources with known redshifts—J0323+0534, J1135−0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123−0112, and J2325−0344—are classified as CSOs because they have double-lobed structures smaller than 1 kpc. Based on their morphologies and flux-density variability, J1057+0012, J1600−0037, and J1753+2750 are instead identified as core–jet sources.

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations at 1.6 GHz were conducted for a sample of 19 GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources, 15 of which were drawn from the Parkes Half Jansky sample. The study sought to image the parsec-scale structures of these sources, identify Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and investigate the absorption mechanisms responsible for their characteristic convex radio spectra.

Total-intensity VLBI images were obtained for 17 sources for the first time. Approximately 80% of these sources display compact, double-lobed structures, suggesting a high incidence of confirmed or candidate CSOs within the sample. Six sources with measured redshifts were formally classified as CSOs because their double-lobed structures extend over less than 1 kpc. In contrast, three other sources were identified as core-jet systems based on their asymmetric morphologies and observed flux-density variability.
outputs.L4:
Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations at 1.6 GHz were carried out for 19 GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources from the PHJ sample. The aim was to resolve their parsec-scale radio emission, classify their morphologies, identify Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and explore the physical origin of their characteristically convex radio spectra. Such spectra may result from synchrotron self-absorption within compact emitting regions, free–free absorption by surrounding ionized gas, or a combination of the two processes.

For 17 of the 19 targets, these observations provided the first VLBI images at this frequency. Approximately 80% of the sources exhibit compact double or mini-double-lobe structures, indicating that symmetric, young radio systems are unusually common in the sample. By combining the new morphology information with available spectral and multi-frequency data, six objects were confirmed as CSOs. Their radio emission is dominated by two oppositely directed lobes or hotspots on either side of the central engine, consistent with intrinsically compact radio galaxies in an early stage of evolution. Several additional double-lobed sources remain strong CSO candidates but require further observations to locate their cores or measure hotspot motions.

Three sources were instead classified as core–jet systems on the basis of their asymmetric, one-sided structures and the likely identification of a compact core. The remaining objects could not be assigned definitive classifications with the available data. Overall, the high fraction of mini-double morphologies demonstrates that the PHJ GPS sample is an efficient reservoir for discovering CSOs. The resolved structures also provide important constraints on the absorption mechanisms responsible for the spectral turnovers, although broader multi-frequency VLBI coverage is needed to distinguish reliably between synchrotron self-absorption and external free–free absorption in individual sources.
outputs.L5:
### Aims and Methods of VLBI

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) is an astronomical technique used to observe distant radio sources with exceptionally high angular resolution. Its main aims include studying active galactic nuclei, mapping the surroundings of black holes, measuring the motion of stars and spacecraft, and determining precise distances within the Universe. VLBI also contributes to geodesy by monitoring Earth’s rotation, tectonic plate movements, and changes in the terrestrial reference frame.

The method combines observations from radio telescopes located far apart, sometimes on different continents or in space. Each telescope records incoming radio signals together with highly accurate timing information provided by atomic clocks. The recorded data are then transferred to a central facility, where they are synchronized and correlated. By analyzing differences in the signals’ arrival times, researchers effectively create a virtual telescope whose diameter is comparable to the maximum distance between the participating antennas. This large baseline enables VLBI to produce extremely detailed images and highly precise positional measurements that cannot be achieved with a single telescope.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise astronomy paper abstract with “Aims and Methods” and “Results” sections describing 1.6 GHz VLBI observations of 19 GHz-Peaked-Spectrum radio sources from the Parkes Half Jansky sample and a previous observing list.
counterfactuals.output:
**Aims and Methods.** We investigate the parsec-scale structure of 19 GHz-peaked-spectrum (GPS) radio sources selected from the Parkes Half-Jansky sample and an earlier observing list. The targets were imaged with 1.6 GHz very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), providing milliarcsecond resolution. Source compactness, component geometry, and recovered flux density were used to assess their morphology and evolutionary status.

**Results.** Most sources are dominated by compact VLBI-scale emission, although their structures range from unresolved objects to one-sided core–jet systems and compact doubles. Several double or symmetric sources are candidate compact symmetric objects, consistent with young radio galaxies, while the core–jet morphologies likely represent beamed active galactic nuclei. The morphological diversity shows that spectral selection alone does not produce a homogeneous population and that multifrequency VLBI observations are required for secure classification.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

The VLBI study observed **19 GHz-peaked-spectrum (GPS) radio sources at 1.6 GHz**. Its main findings were:

- **15 of 19 sources—about 80%—showed compact mini-double or triple-lobed structures.**
- Four were identified as **Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs)**:  
  **J0913+1454, J1111+1955, J1230+1223, and J1436+4820.**
- Four showed **core–jet morphology**:  
  **J0003+2129, J0005+0524, J0620+2102, and J0754+5324.**

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an abstract reporting first-time 1.6 GHz VLBI images of 17 GPS sources, emphasizing the search for CSOs and the possible absorption mechanisms behind their convex radio spectra.
counterfactuals.output: We present the first 1.6 GHz very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) images of a sample of 17 GHz-peaked-spectrum (GPS) radio sources. The milliarcsecond-resolution observations resolve most targets into compact components and provide new constraints on their parsec-scale structures. We use component morphology, symmetry, separation, and available spectral information to identify compact symmetric object (CSO) candidates and to distinguish them from core–jet systems. Several sources show double or triple structures consistent with young radio galaxies whose jets remain confined to sub-kiloparsec scales, although multifrequency VLBI observations are required for secure classifications and core identifications. The data also bear on the origin of the characteristic convex GPS spectra. Synchrotron self-absorption in compact, high-brightness-temperature components can plausibly account for the spectral turnover in some objects, whereas asymmetric structures and evidence for differential obscuration suggest that free–free absorption by ionized circumnuclear gas may be important in others. These results expand the population of candidate CSOs and demonstrate that both intrinsic synchrotron opacity and external absorption should be considered when interpreting GPS spectral peaks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce the aims, methods, and main results for a radio astronomy paper showing that about 80% of a 19-source GPS sample have compact double-lobe morphologies, suggesting a high incidence of CSOs and predominantly edge-on host AGNs.
counterfactuals.output:
**Aim:**  
To determine the parsec-scale structures of a complete 19-source sample of GHz-peaked-spectrum (GPS) radio sources and assess whether they are predominantly compact symmetric objects (CSOs), as expected if GPS sources are young radio galaxies viewed near the plane of the sky.

**Methods:**  
The sources were imaged with high-resolution VLBI observations. Component morphologies, flux densities, sizes, and radio spectra were used to distinguish flat-spectrum cores from steep-spectrum jets and lobes and to classify each object as a compact double, triple/CSO, core–jet source, or unresolved source.

**Main results:**  
Approximately 80% of the sample—about 15 of 19 sources—showed compact double- or triple-lobed structures, making them strong CSO or CSO-candidate systems. Only a small minority displayed the one-sided core–jet morphology typical of strongly beamed AGNs. The unusually high CSO fraction supports the interpretation that GPS sources are young, intrinsically compact radio galaxies whose jets are generally oriented close to the plane of the sky; consequently, their host AGNs are viewed predominantly edge-on rather than along the jet axis.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
